changelog.description: Initial library: universal phrase-level buzzwords, hedges, filler openers, overused transitions, universal structural patterns, and the ten spec-specific anti-patterns.

entries.suggested_fix: Name the actual mechanism, number, or decision instead of the adjective — e.g. replace 'highly scalable' with the concrete scaling approach and its limits.
Delete the hedge and state the point directly — a spec should assert, not soften.

terms: At the end of the day
entries.suggested_fix: Cut the filler opener and start the section with the actual decision, constraint, or requirement.
Remove the transition or replace it with a plain conjunction ('and', 'but') — these read as templated connective tissue rather than reasoning.

entries.description: Section opens with a generic claim ('This section covers...', 'X is a critical part of...') instead of leading with the specific decision, constraint, or requirement the section exists to convey.
entries.suggested_fix: Delete the generic lead-in and open with the concrete decision or constraint itself.

entries.description: Section closes by restating what was just said ('In summary, this ensures...') instead of adding a new decision, open question, or next step.
entries.suggested_fix: Cut the restatement, or replace it with a genuinely new closing item (an open question, a dependency, or a decision still pending).

entries.description: Every section is roughly the same length regardless of how complex or trivial its subject actually is — a sign of padding to match a template rather than writing to the substance.
entries.suggested_fix: Shorten sections covering simple/settled decisions; expand only the sections with real complexity or ambiguity.

entries.description: Stacked-fragment emphasis cadence — short declarative fragments used for rhetorical effect instead of information density (e.g. 'Faster. Simpler. Better.').
entries.suggested_fix: Replace the fragment stack with one sentence that states the actual claim and, if possible, a number backing it.

entries.description: No concrete number, named dependency, or firsthand constraint appears anywhere in the section — every statement floats at the same generic level of abstraction.
entries.suggested_fix: Add at least one concrete anchor: a number, a named library/service/endpoint, or a stated constraint the team actually has to work within.

entries.description: Unquantified claims — a scale, performance, or volume claim with no attached number.
entries.suggested_fix: Require a number: "The system must support 10,000 concurrent users at p95 latency under 300ms." Where no number is known, insert [SPECIFY: expected scale] rather than inventing one.

entries.description: Unfalsifiable requirements — a requirement phrased as a subjective feeling with no way to check it was met.
entries.suggested_fix: Restate as a testable behavior: "A first-time user completes onboarding in under 3 steps with no external help."

entries.description: Hand-wavy technical claims — a feature attributed to "AI" or a named technology with no method specified.
entries.example: "The app leverages AI to personalize recommendations."
entries.suggested_fix: Name the actual method or approach, or insert [SPECIFY: model/approach] if it genuinely isn't decided yet.

entries.description: Happy-path-only coverage — a workflow, user story, or API contract section describes only the successful case, with no failure, error, or edge-case states.
entries.example: A checkout flow section that describes only a successful payment, with no declined-card, timeout, or retry behavior.
entries.suggested_fix: Add the failure/error states alongside the happy path: what the user sees, and what the system does, when the operation fails.

entries.description: Generic/interchangeable personas — a user story written with no distinguishing detail, interchangeable with any other product's persona.
entries.example: "As a user, I want to manage my data, so that I can stay organized."
entries.suggested_fix: Ground the story in this product's actual persona and their specific goal: name who they are, what they're trying to accomplish, and why it matters to them here.

entries.description: Non-measurable NFRs — a non-functional requirement (availability, performance, security) with no attached number or standard.
entries.suggested_fix: Attach a number or named standard: "99.9% monthly uptime" or "complies with OWASP ASVS Level 2".

entries.description: Checkbox-theater acceptance criteria — an acceptance criterion that just restates the feature name rather than describing a testable condition.
entries.suggested_fix: Rewrite as Given/When/Then: "Given a logged-in user on the dashboard, When they click Export, Then a CSV download starts within 2 seconds."

entries.description: Boilerplate section recycling — a section (most often Security or Compliance) reads as generic enough that it could be pasted unchanged into an unrelated product's spec, with nothing tying it to this product's actual data or threat model.
entries.example: A Security section listing "use HTTPS, hash passwords, validate input" with no mention of what this product's data actually is or who could misuse it.
entries.suggested_fix: Tie every control back to this product's specific data, users, and threat model rather than a generic checklist.

entries.description: Fabricated precision — an invented percentage, benchmark, or statistic with no source given in the draft's own input material.
entries.example: "This reduces onboarding time by 47%." with no source for the figure.
entries.suggested_fix: Remove the invented number, or replace it with [SPECIFY: source/benchmark for this figure] if a real figure is expected to exist.

entries.description: Scope-creep escape hatches — core functionality punted to "TBD" or a later phase without an explicit, separate scoping decision to do so.
entries.example: "Refund handling: TBD." inside the core checkout flow section.
entries.suggested_fix: Either specify the behavior now, or make the deferral an explicit, justified scoping decision rather than a silent gap.
